name: VIDEO KILLED THE RADICCHIO STAR BURGER

recipe.history:
Radicchio is a member of the chicory family and one of the most dramatic vegetables in the Italian culinary canon, prized for its jewel-toned burgundy leaves shot through with white veins and its assertive, pleasantly bitter flavor. It is native to the Veneto region of northeastern Italy, particularly the areas around Treviso and Chioggia, where it has been cultivated since at least the fifteenth century. The Treviso variety, long and tapered like a small red romaine, is considered the aristocrat of radicchios; the Chioggia type, round and tight as a small cabbage head, is the most widely exported and the one most commonly found in American markets. Italian farmers have long valued radicchio not just for its flavor but for its hardiness — it thrives in cool autumn temperatures and was traditionally harvested after the first frost, which mellows its bitterness and deepens its sweetness. The plant's vivid color comes from anthocyanins, the same pigments found in red wine and blueberries, and those compounds bring both antioxidant properties and a complex, slightly tannic flavor profile.

Radicchio made its way into American kitchens gradually, first appearing on upscale restaurant menus in the 1980s as part of the wave of Italian regional cuisine that chefs like Marcella Hazan and later Mario Batali popularized with American audiences. For years it was used mainly in salads and as a garnish, its bitterness often softened with balsamic vinegar and a drizzle of olive oil. It wasn't until the grilling craze of the late 1990s and early 2000s that cooks discovered what fire does to radicchio: the heat caramelizes the natural sugars, chars the outer leaves into crispy, smoky ribbons, and transforms the bitterness into something mellow and almost sweet. On a burger, grilled or seared radicchio functions as both a textural element and a flavor counterweight — its slight bitterness cuts through the richness of beef fat in the way that a bitter aperitif clears the palate. Paired with a sweet-savory glaze and a sharp aged cheese, it gives the burger the complexity of a composed restaurant dish.

I first encountered radicchio on a burger at a little place in Portland that had no business being as good as it was — a counter spot with four stools and a menu written on a chalkboard that changed daily. They served a patty melt variation with shaved radicchio that had been wilted briefly in the beef drippings and then deglazed with a splash of balsamic. I remember being suspicious. I had only ever eaten radicchio raw in salads and found it aggressively bitter in that context, the kind of thing you eat because it is good for you rather than because you want to. But when it hit the pan fat and the balsamic, something transformed. It went soft and yielding, the bitterness retreating to the background, and what came forward was this winey, almost fruity depth that made the burger taste like it had been cooking for hours. I drove back to that restaurant three times in one week trying to recreate it in my memory so I could make it at home.

There is only one temperature for a beef patty, and that temperature is medium rare. The internal thermometer should read 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — 54 to 57 degrees Celsius — and it should be pulled from the heat and rested before it climbs any higher. I say this not as ideology but as craft: radicchio, with its slight bitterness and its high water content, needs the juice of a medium-rare patty to truly integrate with the burger. When you cut into a properly cooked patty, the pinkish, iron-rich juices run into the balsamic-glazed radicchio and create a sauce that no recipe can fully replicate. An overcooked patty is a dry patty, and a dry patty with bitter greens is simply a grim eating experience. Medium rare is the only answer. It always has been.
ingredients: 1 egg beaten with 1 tbsp water (egg wash)
1 medium head radicchio, quartered through the core
1/3 cup walnut halves, toasted and roughly chopped
instructions: 1. Make the bun dough: Dissolve yeast and sugar in warm water and milk in a stand mixer bowl. Let sit 5 minutes until foamy. Add egg, butter, salt, and flour. Mix with dough hook on medium 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.
2. Transfer to an oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 4 balls, shape into bun disks, place on parchment-lined sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes.
3. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush buns with egg wash and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool completely.

4. Make the gorgonzola cream: Combine gorgonzola and heavy cream in a small saucepan over low heat, stirring until the cheese melts into a smooth sauce. Stir in thyme. Season to taste. Keep warm over very low heat.
5. Toast the walnuts: Heat a dry skillet over medium heat. Add walnuts and toast 3–4 minutes, tossing frequently, until fragrant. Toss with olive oil and sea salt. Set aside.

6. Grill or sear the radicchio: Heat a cast-iron skillet or grill pan over high heat. Brush radicchio quarters with olive oil and season with salt and pepper. Place cut-side down and cook 2–3 minutes until charred. Flip and cook the other cut side 2 minutes. Transfer to a plate. Whisk balsamic vinegar with honey and drizzle over the hot radicchio. Let sit — the leaves will continue to wilt and absorb the glaze.
7. Form the patties: Divide beef into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Form into patties about 3/4 inch thick with a thumb dimple in the center. Season both sides generously with salt and pepper.
8. Sear the patties in the same cast-iron skillet over high heat, 3 minutes per side undisturbed. Check internal temperature — pull at 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes.
9. While patties rest, lay prosciutto slices in the skillet for 30–45 seconds per side until lightly crisped. Remove.
10. Split buns and toast cut-side down in the skillet for 60 seconds.

11. Assemble: Spoon a pool of gorgonzola cream on the bottom bun. Add the medium-rare patty. Drape a quarter of balsamic-glazed radicchio over the patty, followed by a slice of crisped prosciutto. Scatter toasted walnuts over the top. Finish with flaky sea salt and place the top bun. Serve immediately.
